My husband slid a jar of pickles across the kitchen table one Thursday morning last spring.
He set it down by my coffee, lid pointed up at me.
Then he went back to his eggs.
And he didn't say a word about it.
For 41 years, opening jars was his job.
I never asked him to make it his.
It was just the way our kitchen ran.
The garbage was his, the folding was mine.
So I looked at the jar a second.
Then I gave the lid a twist, and it went.
I set a pickle on his plate like it was nothing at all.
Neither of us mentioned it.
But I'd been married too long for a thing like that not to snag on me.
Dale had opened every jar in that house for 41 years.
He wouldn't just slide one across the table for me to do unless he'd already tried it out in the pantry, where I couldn't see, and it wouldn't give.
He'd sooner pass it over than say so.
I washed up the breakfast dishes and couldn't get that jar out of my head.
Because Dale had opened that exact brand a thousand times.
And that morning he decided, before he ever pulled out his chair, that he wasn't even going to try.
Let me back up and tell you about Dale.
We've been married 41 years.
He's 68, and he retired 3 years ago from the county water department.
Now he's a gardener, and I mean serious about it.
Tomatoes, pole beans, three kinds of peppers, and a compost pile he guards like the family silver.
I raised our three kids and worked the front desk of a dentist's office for 22 years.
So I've spent my life watching people across a counter, keeping track of what's off about them.
Remember that about me.
That kitchen table has been ours for most of our marriage.
We've eaten most every breakfast of our lives at it, the two of us across from each other.
I came to know that man at a table like that.
We each took up the little jobs over the years, without either of us ever deciding who got what.
He salts his eggs before he's tasted them.
Opening the jars was his, for as long as we've had that table.
It was one of the ways he loved me, tho

The door opened, and the screen squeaked on its hinges. Cassidy didn’t turn back and didn’t slow, but a voice called out. “Can I help you?”
It was a voice she knew. A voice her dreams still produced.
No, no, no. That was the last thing she needed.
Without turning, she called, “Sorry. Just took a wrong turn.”
Nearly jogging, she waited for the door to open again and slam, proof the person and gone back inside. Instead, the thud of feet on the patio stairs followed.
He couldn’t be chasing her.
Maybe he wouldn’t recognize her. Maybe, if she stopped him before he got too close, he wouldn’t see her beyond her cap, her new haircut, and her new hair color.
Everything about her was new.
She turned suddenly, hoping he’d stop where he was. “Didn’t mean to interrupt you. I’ll just—“
“Cassidy?”
She wanted to laugh it off, give her fake name, pretend. But the words were caught.
Her sunglasses hung uselessly from her hand. She should have slipped them back on. Stupid mistake. Fatal mistake.
He was there, just ten, maybe fifteen feet from her. He looked so different. The clean-cut high school jock now had long hair, a mustache, and a beard. He’d broadened, matured. But the eyes… Those milk chocolate eyes hadn’t changed, even if they were filled with malice right now.
“What are—?” He closed the distance between them. When he was inches from her, he froze. “What are you doing here?”
She swallowed all the emotions trying to climb out of her throat. Fear, affection, grief.
Love.

I set a pickle on his plate like it was nothing at all.

I washed up the breakfast dishes and couldn't get that jar out of my head.  
  
Because Dale had opened that exact brand a thousand times.  
  
And that morning he decided, before he ever pulled out his chair, that he wasn't even going to try.  
  
Let me back up and tell you about Dale.  
  
We've been married 41 years.  
  
He's 68, and he retired 3 years ago from the county water department.  
  
Now he's a gardener, and I mean serious about it.  
  
Tomatoes, pole beans, three kinds of peppers, and a compost pile he guards like the family silver.  
  
I raised our three kids and worked the front desk of a dentist's office for 22 years.  
  
So I've spent my life watching people across a counter, keeping track of what's off about them.  
  
Remember that about me.  
  
That kitchen table has been ours for most of our marriage.  
  
We've eaten most every breakfast of our lives at it, the two of us across from each other.  
  
I came to know that man at a table like that.  
  
We each took up the little jobs over the years, without either of us ever deciding who got what.  
  
He salts his eggs before he's tasted them.  
  
Opening the jars was his, for as long as we've had that table.  
  
It was one of the ways he loved me, though neither of us would ever have put it that way.  
  
A jar I couldn't budge would come to him at the counter, and he'd plant his feet and work it till it gave.  
  
Then he'd hand it back open and never look up from what he was doing.  
  
A whole marriage of that.  
  
So small neither of us ever gave it a thought, till the morning it stopped.  
  
I came by the noticing honestly, years before that jar.  
  
The front desk of a dentist's office taught me to read people.  
  
I sat there year after year and learned to size a person up while they were still filling out the clipboard.  
  
The man cracking jokes about the drill is the one scared half to death.  
  
More than once I watched a woman swear she felt fine while she held her jaw so it wouldn't shake.  
  
So I trust that part of me, the part that catches what's off.  
  
It's almost never wrong.  
  
And that spring, something about Dale had started to bother me.  
  
The jar made three.
